newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK oil shares hit record highs on results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK oil shares hit record highs on results.

text.p: Shares in integrated UK oil companies powered to record highs on Wednesday, bolstered by Tuesday's British Petroleum Plc results and confidence about Thursday's earnings from Shell Transport and Trading Group Plc.
Relatively buoyant crude oil prices and investors pouring into defensive UK stocks also allowed BP and Shell to contribute about half of the FTSE 100's 44-point gain by midday, analysts said.

By 1115 GMT, BP shares were up 22p to 883-1/2p and Shell gained 17-1/2p to 475-1/2p, and the two were among the most active stocks in the blue-chip index. Burmah Castrol Plc shares gained 11p to 10.78-1/2 stg.

"We saw some results from the U.S. majors that were above expectations and BP was well above, so people are thinking Shell could also report above expectations," said Shawn Reynolds, equities research analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Anglo-Dutch giant Royal Dutch/Shell Group is expected to post net income between 1.265 billion and 1.48 billion sterling for the second quarter, analysts said.
The group reported comparative earnings of 1.187 sterling in the same 1996 quarter.
"I think the market is looking for Shell to come in with results that are at the top end of expectations, if not above them," said Mark Iannotti, oil analyst at BZW.
"Underpinning the results season for the two majors is a very firm crude price...and the upstream exposure makes the results very robust," he said.

Brent crude oil futures on the International Petroleum Exchange are trading just above $19 a barrel for September delivery. That is below where the spot contract was trading a year ago, near $21-$22, but above this year's low near $17.50.

The sector continued to garner support from BP's sparkling results when it reported second-quarter profits of 740 million pounds, against the most optimistic analysts' forecasts of 690 million pounds.

BP also said it planned to buy back some $500 million worth of shares before the 1998 annual shareholders meeting. The oil company will then seek approval for a broader policy to buy-back shares from "time to time".
"Everybody is going to have to raise BP's estimates for 1997 if not for 1998," Reynolds said.
"The share buy-back is a very strong sign that the management feels it will comfortably meet its own aggressive financial targets and in typical BP fashion, will exceed them," he said.
Despite Shell's share gain, Reynolds has a "hold" rating on the stock and BZW a "sell".
Reynolds rates BP an "outperform", and Iannotti said BZW was a buyer.
